decks.title: Our Constitution — Part 1: Meaning, Adoption, Citizenship and Voting
goals: Define a constitution and explain why a country needs one
State the dates of adoption and enforcement and explain why 26 January was chosen
Explain single citizenship and contrast it with dual citizenship in the United States
Explain universal adult franchise and the minimum voting age

slides.heading: Our Constitution: Meaning, Adoption and Salient Features
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what a **constitution** is, when ours was **adopted** and **enforced**, and how it gives every adult one **citizenship** and one **vote**.

nodes.label: Meaning and need of a constitution

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the meaning and need of a constitution, adoption and enforcement, single citizenship, and universal adult franchise
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every country runs on rules. In this chapter we study the rulebook of India, our Constitution. In this first part we ask what a constitution is and why a country needs one, when ours was adopted and when it came into force, why Indians have one citizenship only, and how every adult citizen gets a vote.

slides.heading: What is a constitution?
slides.body_md: A **constitution** is the **fundamental law** of a country: the basic rulebook for the government and the people.

rows: the organs of government: who makes, carries out and judges the laws
the power of every office, so no ruler can do as he or she pleases
the rights of the people against misuse of power
disputes by giving all a common set of rules

visual.alt: Table of four jobs of a constitution: it sets up the organs of government, limits their power, protects rights and settles disputes

slides.narration: A constitution is the basic law of a country. It does four jobs. It sets up the organs of government, the bodies that make, carry out and judge the laws. It limits the power of each office. It protects the rights of the people. And it gives everyone a common set of rules to settle disputes.

slides.heading: Why does a country need a constitution?
slides.body_md: Think of a game with no written rules: whoever holds the ball decides everything.

visual.alt: Flow showing why a constitution is needed: with no written rules rulers decide everything, so rights are unsafe and a constitution is needed
visual.caption: Why a country needs a constitution.

slides.narration: Imagine a game with no written rules. The strongest player would decide everything. A country without a constitution is like that. Rulers could decide everything, and the rights of the people would be unsafe. A constitution makes the rules known to all, so that power is limited and rights are protected, and the country can stay stable.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the island of Tarangia
slides.body_md: In the imagined island state of Tarangia the ruler alone decides how long he rules and whom to punish.
bullets: Step 1 — Spot the problem: no limits on power.
Step 2 — Link to a need: a constitution must limit rulers.
Step 3 — Add a second need: it must protect the rights of the people.
Step 4 — Conclude: Tarangia needs a written constitution.

rows: People punished without a fair rule
Protect rights and give a fair process

visual.alt: Table linking two situations in the imagined island of Tarangia to the needs of a constitution: limiting power and protecting rights

slides.narration: Let us apply this to an imagined island called Tarangia. The ruler decides how long he stays in power and whom he will punish. First, spot the problem: nothing limits his power. Second, link it to a need: a constitution must limit rulers. Third, add that it must protect rights. So we conclude that Tarangia needs a written constitution.

slides.heading: The Constituent Assembly
slides.body_md: The **Constituent Assembly** framed our Constitution. It first met on **9 December 1946**.

rows: Framed the Constitution; first met on 9 December 1946
Prepared the draft that the Assembly discussed and adopted

visual.alt: Table of the Constituent Assembly with its first meeting, its President, the chairman of the Drafting Committee and the work of that committee

slides.narration: The Constitution was framed by a body called the Constituent Assembly. It first met on 9 December 1946. Doctor Rajendra Prasad was its President. A Drafting Committee, chaired by Doctor Bhimrao Ambedkar, prepared the draft, which the Assembly discussed in detail over nearly three years before adopting it.

slides.body_md: Adoption and enforcement are **two events** about two months apart.

slides.narration: Look at the timeline. The Assembly first met in December 1946. It adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949, a day now observed as Constitution Day. But the Constitution came into force only on 26 January 1950, about two months later. Adoption means the Assembly accepted the text; enforcement means it began to apply.

slides.heading: Quick check: the first meeting
slides.body_md: In which year did the Constituent Assembly first meet?
slides.narration: Remember the timeline. The first meeting came before independence.

slides.heading: Why 26 January?
slides.body_md: The date **26 January 1950** was chosen to recall **26 January 1930**, observed as **Independence Day** after the call for **Purna Swaraj** (complete independence).

nodes.label: Purna Swaraj declared as the goal
26 January 1950: the Constitution comes into force

visual.alt: Flow: Purna Swaraj declared as the goal, 26 January 1930 observed as Independence Day, and 26 January 1950 chosen for the Constitution to come into force
visual.caption: Why 26 January was chosen.

slides.narration: Why did the framers wait until 26 January? In 1930 the nation had demanded Purna Swaraj, which means complete independence, and had observed 26 January as Independence Day. By bringing the Constitution into force on the same date in 1950, the framers honoured that pledge. Note that independence itself came earlier, in 1947.

slides.heading: Quick check: adopted or enforced?
slides.body_md: True or false: adopted and enforced on one day.
slides.narration: Ask yourself whether adoption and enforcement were the same event.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: planning a 10-mark answer
slides.body_md: Question: (i) What is a constitution? Give two reasons for it. [3] (ii) Name the President of the Assembly, the Drafting Committee chairman and the first meeting date. [3] (iii) Give both dates and explain 26 January. [4]
bullets: (i) Definition + two needs.
(ii) Two names with posts + 9 December 1946.
(iii) 26 November 1949 and 26 January 1950 + the Purna Swaraj link.
Write one clear point for every mark.

rows: Definition of a constitution + two reasons
Both dates + the Purna Swaraj reason

visual.alt: Table planning a three-part ten-mark answer on the Constitution: part (i) three marks, part (ii) three marks, part (iii) four marks, with the points for each part

slides.narration: Here is how to plan a ten mark answer in three parts. For part one, give the definition and two needs. For part two, name the President of the Assembly and the chairman of the Drafting Committee, and add the date of the first meeting. For part three, give both dates and explain the choice of 26 January. Write one clear point for every mark.

slides.heading: Single citizenship
slides.body_md: In India every citizen is a citizen of **India only**. The United States has **dual** citizenship: the nation and a State.

visual.caption: Single and dual citizenship (schematic, not to scale).

slides.narration: India is a federation of States, yet a citizen of India belongs to the nation alone. There is no separate State citizenship. In the United States it is different. A person is a citizen of the nation and also a citizen of the State in which he or she lives. That is called dual citizenship.

slides.heading: Single citizenship builds unity
bullets: Same **status** wherever a citizen lives.
A common **national identity** above regional identities.
Easier **movement and settlement** across States.
Note: Overseas Citizenship of India is **not** dual citizenship: it gives privileges but no vote.

rows: No: only one citizenship, of India
If I move to another State?
National unity and a common identity

visual.alt: Table of four questions about single citizenship and the answers for India, including that Overseas Citizenship of India is not dual citizenship

slides.narration: Single citizenship supports unity. A citizen has the same status in every State, so nobody is an outsider in another part of the country. It builds a common national identity above regional ones, and it makes it easy to move and settle anywhere. One more point: Overseas Citizenship of India is not dual citizenship. It gives privileges, but not the vote.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: Meera moves to Gujarat
slides.body_md: Meera, born in Assam, takes a job in Gujarat. What is her citizenship?
bullets: Step 1 — Identify the system: India.
Step 2 — Single or dual? Single citizenship.
Step 3 — Apply: no Assam or Gujarat citizenship exists.
Step 4 — Conclude: she is a citizen of India, nothing more and nothing less.

visual.alt: Flow of the method for citizenship problems: identify the system, decide single or dual, apply it to the person and state the conclusion
visual.caption: Method for citizenship problems.

slides.narration: Try this method. Meera, born in Assam, takes a job in Gujarat. First identify the system: India. Second, is it single or dual? It is single. Third, apply it: there is no Assam citizenship and no Gujarat citizenship to gain or lose. So Meera is simply a citizen of India, wherever she lives.

slides.body_md: Arrange the four events in the order in which they took place.
slides.narration: Start from the first meeting of the Assembly and move forward to the Fundamental Duties.

slides.heading: Universal adult franchise
slides.body_md: **Universal adult franchise**: every adult citizen has the right to vote, whatever their caste, religion, sex, education or wealth.

visual.alt: Table comparing a limited franchise in an imagined kingdom with universal adult franchise: who votes, the conditions and the value of a vote

slides.narration: Universal adult franchise means that every adult citizen has the right to vote. It does not matter whether the person is rich or poor, educated or not, man or woman, or of any caste or religion. Compare this with an imagined kingdom in which only property owning men could vote. Here, one adult has one vote of equal value.

slides.heading: The voting age: 21 to 18
slides.body_md: The **61st Amendment** (1988) lowered the minimum voting age from **21** to **18** years; it took effect in **1989**.

slides.narration: At first the minimum voting age was twenty one. In 1988 the sixty first Amendment lowered it to eighteen years, and the change took effect in 1989. Young adults, many of them students or first time workers, gained a voice in choosing their government. Remember, an eligible citizen must also be registered on the electoral roll.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: reading a voters list
slides.body_md: An imagined voters list names Kavita (18), Gopal (52, landless, cannot read) and Ravi (17). Who is eligible?
bullets: Step 1 — Check citizenship and age only.
Step 2 — Kavita is 18: eligible.
Step 3 — Gopal is an adult: eligible, since education and property do not matter.
Step 4 — Ravi is 17: not yet eligible.

rows: Literacy and property do not matter

visual.alt: Table applying the voting rules to three imagined people: Kavita aged 18 and Gopal aged 52 are eligible, Ravi aged 17 is not

slides.narration: Let us read an imagined voters list. The test is simple: citizenship and age. Kavita is eighteen, so she can vote. Gopal is fifty two. He owns no land and cannot read, but that does not matter, so he can vote. Ravi is seventeen, so he must wait until he turns eighteen.

slides.heading: Quick check: which amendment?
slides.body_md: Which amendment lowered the voting age?
slides.narration: Remember the year, nineteen eighty eight, and which amendment number belongs to the voting age.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: A **constitution** sets up, limits and protects; it is needed to control power and safeguard rights.
**Adopted** 26 November 1949; **in force** 26 January 1950 (Purna Swaraj link).
**Single citizenship**: India only; the United States has dual citizenship.
**Universal adult franchise**: every adult citizen votes; age 18 since 1989 (61st Amendment).

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: the constitution as basic law, adopted on 26 November 1949, in force on 26 January 1950, single citizenship and the vote at 18
visual.caption: Part 1 in five steps.

slides.narration: To sum up. A constitution is the basic law that sets up, limits and protects. Ours was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950. India has single citizenship, unlike the dual citizenship of the United States. And every adult citizen has a vote, with the minimum age at eighteen since 1989.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Keep **adoption** (26 November 1949) apart from **enforcement** (26 January 1950).
Never write that India has State citizenship.
Do not add education or property conditions to the vote.
Mention **Purna Swaraj** when explaining 26 January.
In 3 + 3 + 4 questions give one clear point for each mark.

rows: Adopted and enforced on one day
26 Nov 1949 and 26 Jan 1950 are two events

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and the correct version of each

slides.narration: Some common slips. Do not mix up adoption and enforcement; they are two events about two months apart. Never say that India has State citizenship. The vote does not depend on education or property. And when you explain why 26 January was chosen, always mention Purna Swaraj. In structured questions, write one clear point for each mark.

decks.title: Our Constitution — Part 2: Fundamental Rights and Fundamental Duties
goals: Explain what makes a right fundamental and why such rights are justiciable
Name the six categories of Fundamental Rights with an example of each
State when and how the Fundamental Duties were added and list five of them

slides.heading: Fundamental Rights and Fundamental Duties
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the **rights** the Constitution guarantees, how they are **enforced**, and the **duties** that go with them.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: what makes a right fundamental, the six categories, Constitutional Remedies and the Fundamental Duties
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we study two of the best known features of the Constitution. First, the Fundamental Rights: what makes a right fundamental, the six categories and how courts protect them. Then the Fundamental Duties: when they were added, what they ask of us, and how they go hand in hand with our rights.

slides.heading: What makes a right fundamental?
slides.body_md: A **Fundamental Right** is guaranteed by the Constitution itself and is **justiciable**: a court can enforce it.

rows: Created by a law of the legislature
Directly in the Supreme Court or a High Court
Through ordinary courts under that law

visual.alt: Table comparing a Fundamental Right with an ordinary legal right by source, enforcement and how it can be changed

slides.narration: A right is fundamental when the Constitution itself guarantees it. Ordinary legal rights are created by laws, and a later law can change them. Fundamental Rights can be changed only by a constitutional amendment. They are also justiciable, which means that if one is violated a citizen can go straight to the Supreme Court or a High Court.

slides.body_md: There are **6** categories as of 2024.

visual.caption: The six categories of Fundamental Rights (as of 2024).

slides.narration: There are six categories of Fundamental Rights today. They are the Right to Equality, the Right to Freedom, the Right against Exploitation, the Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and the Right to Constitutional Remedies. Each protects a different part of life, as you can see from the example under each name.

slides.heading: An example for each category

rows: No discrimination on grounds of caste or sex; untouchability abolished
Speech and expression, peaceful assembly, forming associations, movement
Ban on forced labour and on child labour in hazardous work
Freedom to profess, practise and spread one's faith
Minorities may conserve their script and run schools
The right to move the courts to enforce the other rights

visual.alt: Table of the six categories of Fundamental Rights with an example of each

slides.narration: Learn one clear example for each category. Under Equality, no discrimination on grounds of caste or sex. Under Freedom, speech and expression. Under the Right against Exploitation, a ban on forced labour and on child labour in hazardous work. Under Freedom of Religion, the freedom to practise one faith. Under Cultural and Educational Rights, minorities may run schools. And the Right to Constitutional Remedies lets people go to court.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which category?
slides.body_md: In the imagined village of Barauli, children of one hamlet are not allowed to use the common well because of their caste.
bullets: Step 1 — Read the situation: unequal treatment because of caste.
Step 2 — Find the right at stake: equal treatment in public places.
Step 3 — Name the category: Right to Equality.
Step 4 — Give the reason: discrimination on grounds of caste is prohibited.

visual.alt: Flow of the method for classifying a case: read the situation, find the right at stake, name the category and give a reason
visual.caption: Method for case questions.

slides.narration: Here is a method for case questions. In the imagined village of Barauli, children of one hamlet are not allowed to use the common well because of their caste. First read the situation. Then find the right at stake, which is equal treatment. Name the category, the Right to Equality, and give the reason: discrimination on grounds of caste is not allowed.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the cases
slides.body_md: Match each situation with its category.
slides.narration: For each case, find the right at stake and then name the category.

slides.heading: Right to Constitutional Remedies
slides.body_md: A citizen whose right is violated can **move the Supreme Court or a High Court**; the court can order the right to be enforced.

nodes.label: Citizen moves the Supreme Court or a High Court
Court orders the right to be enforced

visual.alt: Flow of the Right to Constitutional Remedies: a right is violated, the citizen moves a court, the court hears the case and orders enforcement
visual.caption: Why rights are justiciable.

slides.narration: What good is a right if nobody can enforce it? The Right to Constitutional Remedies answers this. A citizen whose Fundamental Right is violated can move the Supreme Court or a High Court. The court hears the case and can order that the right be enforced. This is why Fundamental Rights are called justiciable.

slides.heading: Quick check: the way to court
slides.body_md: Which right lets a person approach a court to enforce others?
slides.narration: Look for the right that gives the way to enforce all the others.

slides.heading: Rights have limits, and the list has changed
slides.body_md: Rights are subject to **reasonable restrictions**. The **right to property** was removed from the list by the **44th Amendment (1978)**.

visual.alt: Table: seven categories of Fundamental Rights in 1950 including the right to property, and six since the 44th Amendment of 1978, as of 2024

slides.narration: Fundamental Rights are not absolute. They can be limited by reasonable restrictions, for example in the interest of public order. The list itself has also changed. The right to property was originally included, but the forty fourth Amendment of 1978 removed it. So, as of 2024, there are six categories, not seven.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: is freedom unlimited?
slides.body_md: In a debate at the imagined Riverside School, Anita says her freedom of speech is absolute.
bullets: Step 1 — State the claim: rights are absolute.
Step 2 — Test it: reasonable restrictions exist.
Step 3 — Give a reason: public order and the rights of others.
Step 4 — Conclude: freedom is real but not unlimited.

rows: No: reasonable restrictions apply, such as public order
No: but courts give the final remedy

visual.alt: Table of three claims about Fundamental Rights and the verdict on each

slides.narration: Let us test a claim. In a debate at the imagined Riverside School, Anita says her freedom of speech is absolute. Step one, state the claim. Step two, test it: the Constitution allows reasonable restrictions. Step three, give a reason, such as public order and the rights of others. So her freedom is real, but not unlimited.

slides.heading: Fundamental Duties: how they came
slides.body_md: Added in **1976** by the **42nd Amendment** on the recommendation of the **Swaran Singh Committee**; **eleven** since the **86th Amendment (2002)**.

slides.narration: The original Constitution did not list duties. In 1976 the forty second Amendment added a list of Fundamental Duties, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee. There were ten at first. In 2002 the eighty sixth Amendment added an eleventh, so as of 2024 there are eleven.

slides.heading: The eleven duties in short

rows: Respect the Constitution, flag and anthem
Cherish the ideals of the freedom struggle
Defend the country and render national service when called
Promote harmony; give up practices that demean women
Value the heritage of a composite culture
Protect the environment; have compassion for living creatures
Develop scientific temper, humanism, inquiry and reform
Safeguard public property; give up violence
Strive for excellence in individual and collective work
Parents and guardians to give schooling to a child of six to fourteen

visual.alt: Table of the eleven Fundamental Duties in paraphrase with a short example of each

slides.narration: Here are the eleven duties in short. Respect the Constitution, the flag and the anthem. Cherish the ideals of the freedom struggle. Uphold unity and integrity. Defend the country. Promote harmony and respect for women. Value our heritage. Protect the environment. Develop scientific temper. Safeguard public property. Strive for excellence. And the eleventh: parents and guardians give schooling to children aged six to fourteen. Learn them in your own words.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: which duty?
slides.body_md: Match three imagined actions with the duty each fulfils.
bullets: Step 1 — Read the action.
Step 2 — Find the matching duty.
Step 3 — Cleaning the pond protects the environment.
Step 4 — A science club builds scientific temper; repairing a bench safeguards public property.

rows: Repairing a damaged bench in the hall

visual.alt: Table matching three imagined actions with the duty each fulfils: cleaning a pond, a science club and repairing a bench

slides.narration: Apply the duties to actions. Cleaning the school pond protects the environment. Running a science club activity builds scientific temper. Repairing a damaged bench in the hall safeguards public property. For each case, read the action, find the matching duty, and say why in one line.

slides.heading: Quick check: the eleventh duty
slides.body_md: What does the eleventh duty, added in 2002, concern?
slides.narration: Remember that it came with the eighty sixth Amendment and concerns children between six and fourteen.

slides.heading: Duties complement rights
slides.body_md: My **right** is safe only if others respect it, so I have a **duty** to respect theirs. The duties have **no direct court remedy** like rights.

visual.alt: Flow showing that rights and duties are two sides: my right, others respect it, my duty to respect theirs, and rights stay safe for all
visual.caption: Rights and duties go together.

slides.narration: Rights and duties are two sides of one coin. My right is safe only if other people respect it, and theirs is safe only if I respect it. So the duties remind us that rights come with responsibilities. One difference: a citizen cannot go to court to enforce a duty in the way that a right is enforced.

slides.heading: Quick check: rights and duties
slides.body_md: Decide whether the reason explains the assertion.
slides.narration: Ask whether the reason explains why duties complement rights.

bullets: (i) 1976, 42nd Amendment, Swaran Singh Committee, eleven.
(ii) Four duties, one line each.
(iii) The 2002 duty on education + the link with rights.
Give the reason in the last part to earn the final marks.

rows: The eleventh duty (2002) + how duties complement rights

slides.narration: Here is how to plan a ten mark question on the duties. Part one needs the year, the amendment, the committee and the number. Part two asks for four duties, one line each. Part three needs the eleventh duty and an explanation of how duties complement rights. The reason in the last part earns the final marks.

bullets: Fundamental Rights are **guaranteed** and **justiciable**; six categories as of 2024.
The **Right to Constitutional Remedies** lets citizens move the courts.
Rights have **reasonable restrictions**; the right to property was removed in 1978.
**Duties:** 1976, 42nd Amendment, Swaran Singh Committee; eleven since 2002.

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 2: Fundamental Rights are justiciable, six categories as of 2024, the remedy of going to court, duties added in 1976 and eleven duties since 2002
visual.caption: Part 2 in five steps.

slides.narration: To sum up. Fundamental Rights are guaranteed by the Constitution and enforced by courts. There are six categories as of 2024, and the right to property was removed in 1978. The Right to Constitutional Remedies takes us to court. The duties were added in 1976 and are eleven today, and they complement our rights.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 2
bullets: Write **six** categories, and name the right to property as the one removed.
Do not say duties are enforceable like rights.
Give a **rule** or reason when you classify a case.
Learn the order: 1976, 1978, 1988 (effective 1989), 2002.
Paraphrase duties in your own words; do not try to copy the text.

rows: No direct court remedy for duties

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and need of a constitution
sections.body_md:
- A **constitution** is the **fundamental law** of a country.
- It **sets up** the organs of government, **limits** their powers, **protects** the rights of the people and gives common rules for settling disputes.
- Without one, rulers could decide everything and rights would be unsafe.
- India's Constitution was framed by the **Constituent Assembly**, whose President was **Dr Rajendra Prasad**; the **Drafting Committee** was chaired by **Dr B. R. Ambedkar**.

key_terms.definition_md: The fundamental law that sets up and limits government and protects rights.
The committee of the Constituent Assembly that prepared the draft of the Constitution.

rows: the organs of government: who makes, carries out and judges the laws
the power of every office, so no ruler can do as he or she pleases
the rights of the people against misuse of power
disputes by giving all a common set of rules

visual.alt: Table of four jobs of a constitution: it sets up the organs of government, limits their power, protects rights and settles disputes

visuals.alt: Flow showing why a constitution is needed: with no written rules rulers decide everything, so rights are unsafe and a constitution is needed
visuals.caption: Why a country needs a constitution.

sections.heading: 2. Adoption and enforcement
sections.body_md:
- The Assembly **first met on 9 December 1946**.
- The Constitution was **adopted on 26 November 1949** (now observed as **Constitution Day**).
- It **came into force on 26 January 1950**, observed as Republic Day, about two months after adoption.
- **Why 26 January?** On 26 January 1930 Independence Day had been observed after the call for **Purna Swaraj** (complete independence); the framers chose the same date to honour that pledge.

key_terms.definition_md: Acceptance of the final text by the Constituent Assembly (26 November 1949).
The date from which the Constitution began to apply (26 January 1950).

sections.heading: 3. Single citizenship
sections.body_md:
- Every citizen of India is a citizen of **India only**; there is **no separate State citizenship**.
- In a federation like the **United States**, a person is a citizen of the nation and of the State of residence: **dual citizenship**.
- Single citizenship promotes **unity**: one status for all, a common national identity and easy movement across States.
- **Optional note:** Overseas Citizenship of India is a special status with privileges; it is **not** dual citizenship and does not carry the vote.

key_terms.definition_md: One citizenship, of the nation, for every citizen of a federation.
Citizenship of both the nation and a State, as in the United States.

sections.heading: 4. Universal adult franchise
sections.body_md:
- **Universal adult franchise:** every adult citizen can vote, without discrimination of caste, religion, sex, education or wealth.
- The **minimum voting age is 18**. The **61st Amendment (1988)** lowered it from 21, with effect from 1989.
- A voter must also be on the **electoral roll**.
- **Why it strengthens democracy:** political equality (one adult, one vote), a government answerable to all, participation and legitimacy.

sections.heading: 5. Fundamental Rights
sections.body_md:
- **Fundamental** because guaranteed by the Constitution and essential for a person's development; **justiciable**, so courts enforce them.
- **Six categories (as of 2024):** Equality; Freedom; against Exploitation; Freedom of Religion; Cultural and Educational Rights; Constitutional Remedies.
- The **right to property** was removed from the list by the **44th Amendment (1978)**.
- Rights are subject to **reasonable restrictions**, for example in the interest of public order.
- **Constitutional Remedies:** a citizen can move the Supreme Court or a High Court to enforce the other rights.

sections.heading: 6. Fundamental Duties
sections.body_md:
- Added in **1976** by the **42nd Amendment** on the recommendation of the **Swaran Singh Committee**.
- **Eleven** duties as of 2024; the eleventh (parents and guardians to provide education to a child aged **six to fourteen**) was added by the **86th Amendment (2002)**.
- Examples (in paraphrase): respect the Constitution, flag and anthem; protect the environment; safeguard public property; develop scientific temper; promote harmony.
- Duties have **no direct court remedy** like rights, but they **complement** rights: rights are safe only when everyone respects them.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that the Constitution was adopted and enforced on one day.
- Saying that Indians hold State citizenship.
- Adding education or property to the conditions for voting.
- Giving seven Fundamental Rights, or ten duties, without a date.
- Saying that duties are enforced by courts in the same way as rights.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option or term.
- 2 and 3 marks: one clear point per mark.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one clear point per mark; the last part usually needs a reason or an evaluation.

questions.stem_md: A student council in the imagined town of Kaveripur wants to tell Class 6 pupils what a constitution is. Which description should it use?

options.text_md: A list of the new laws that the legislature passes in a single year
The basic law that sets up the organs of government, limits their powers and protects the rights of citizens
A speech in which the head of state announces the plans of the government
The record of the decisions given by courts in past disputes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The basic law that sets up the organs of government, limits their powers and protects the rights of citizens. A constitution is the fundamental law of a country: it creates the organs of government, divides and limits their powers and guarantees rights. A list of yearly laws is ordinary legislation, a speech of plans is a policy statement, and a record of judgments is case law, none of which is the basic framework.

questions.stem_md: On which date did the Constituent Assembly adopt the Constitution of India?

options.text_md: 26 January 1950
15 August 1947
9 December 1946
26 November 1949

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 26 November 1949. 26 November 1949 is the date of adoption, now observed as Constitution Day. 26 January 1950 is the date it came into force, 15 August 1947 is the date of independence, and 9 December 1946 is the date of the first meeting of the Assembly.

questions.stem_md: Why did the framers choose 26 January 1950 as the day on which the Constitution would come into force?

options.text_md: The date recalled the Independence Day that had been observed on 26 January 1930 after the demand for Purna Swaraj
It was the day on which India became independent from British rule
It was the birthday of the President of the Constituent Assembly
It was the day on which the Drafting Committee was first appointed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The date recalled the Independence Day that had been observed on 26 January 1930 after the demand for Purna Swaraj. The date was chosen to honour 26 January 1930, observed as Independence Day after the Purna Swaraj resolution. Independence itself came on 15 August 1947; neither a birthday nor the appointment of the Drafting Committee explains the choice.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined history quiz, the card reads: the Constituent Assembly of India held its first meeting in December of which year?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 1946. The Assembly first met on 9 December 1946. 1947 is the year of independence, 1949 the year of adoption and 1950 the year the Constitution came into force.

questions.stem_md: Who chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly, the committee that prepared the draft of the Constitution?

options.text_md: Dr Rajendra Prasad
Jawaharlal Nehru
Dr B. R. Ambedkar
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Dr B. R. Ambedkar. Dr B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee. Dr Rajendra Prasad was the President of the Constituent Assembly itself; the other two leaders were prominent members but did not chair the Drafting Committee.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined island state of Tarangia there is no written framework: the ruler decides how long to stay in office, what laws to make and which people may speak in public. Which need of a constitution does this situation show most clearly?

options.text_md: The need to limit the power of rulers and protect the rights of the people
The need to raise more revenue from taxes
The need to choose a national flower and bird
The need to replace all elections by appointments

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The need to limit the power of rulers and protect the rights of the people. Where one person decides everything, nothing prevents misuse of power, so a constitution is needed to set limits and guarantee rights. Revenue, national symbols and appointments are not the central reason why a country needs a constitution.

questions.stem_md: In a Class 9 test paper from the imagined Sunrise School, a pupil writes that the Constitution was adopted and enforced on 26 January 1950. Which correction is accurate?

options.text_md: It was adopted on 26 January 1950 and came into force on 26 November 1949
Both events took place on 15 August 1947
Both events took place on 9 December 1946
It was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950. Adoption and enforcement were two separate events about two months apart: adoption on 26 November 1949 and enforcement on 26 January 1950. The reversed order is impossible, and the two other dates mark independence and the first meeting of the Assembly.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by single citizenship in India?

options.text_md: Only one person in each family can be a citizen
Every citizen is a citizen of India only, with no separate citizenship of a State
A citizen may live in one State alone for life
Only one language may be used by citizens

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Every citizen is a citizen of India only, with no separate citizenship of a State. Single citizenship means one citizenship for the whole country, whichever State a person lives in. It says nothing about family members, residence for life or language.

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly contrasts India with the United States of America in the matter of citizenship?

options.text_md: In the United States a person is a citizen of the nation and of the State of residence; in India a person is a citizen of India alone
In India a person is a citizen of the Union and of a State; in the United States, of the nation alone
Both countries give their citizens a separate citizenship of every State
Neither country has any rules on citizenship

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** In the United States a person is a citizen of the nation and of the State of residence; in India a person is a citizen of India alone. The United States has dual citizenship (national and State), while India has single citizenship. The second option reverses the two systems, the third is true of neither country, and every country has some rules on citizenship.

questions.stem_md: Meera, born and educated in Assam, takes up a teaching job in Gujarat. Under the Indian Constitution, which statement about her citizenship is correct?

options.text_md: She becomes a citizen of Gujarat and loses her citizenship of Assam
She remains a citizen of India, with no separate citizenship of Gujarat or Assam
She holds the citizenship of Assam as well as the citizenship of India
She must apply to the Gujarat government for fresh citizenship

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** She remains a citizen of India, with no separate citizenship of Gujarat or Assam. India has single citizenship, so moving between States does not change a citizen's status: there is no State citizenship to lose, keep or apply for. The three wrong options all assume a separate State citizenship, which the Constitution does not create.

questions.stem_md: India is a federation of States, yet it has single citizenship. What is the main purpose of this choice?

options.text_md: To let each State decide who may be called a citizen
To stop people from moving from one State to another
To promote national unity and a common identity among all citizens
To weaken the powers of the Union government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** To promote national unity and a common identity among all citizens. One citizenship for all tells people in every State that they belong to the same nation and share the same status, which supports unity. It does not let States make their own rules, restrict movement or weaken the Union.

questions.stem_md: Dev, who lives abroad, holds an Overseas Citizenship of India card. A friend says that India now allows dual citizenship. Which reply is accurate?

options.text_md: The card makes Dev a full citizen of India with the right to vote
The card makes Dev a citizen of an Indian State as well as of his country of residence
The card proves that the United States and India follow the same system
The card is not dual citizenship: it gives long-term travel and residence privileges but not the right to vote

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The card is not dual citizenship: it gives long-term travel and residence privileges but not the right to vote. India's Constitution is built on single citizenship; an Overseas Citizen of India holds a special status that gives certain privileges but not full citizenship, so no vote. The other options wrongly treat the card as full or State citizenship, or as a copy of the American system.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by universal adult franchise?

options.text_md: Only educated adults may vote
Only adults who pay taxes may vote
Every resident of the country, of any age, may vote
Every adult citizen has the right to vote, without any discrimination of caste, religion, sex, education or wealth

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Every adult citizen has the right to vote, without any discrimination of caste, religion, sex, education or wealth. Universal adult franchise gives each adult citizen one vote, whatever the person's background. Education and tax conditions would make the franchise limited, and children and non-citizens are not covered.

questions.stem_md: What is the minimum age at which an Indian citizen can vote in elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies today?

options.text_md: 21 years
25 years
18 years
16 years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 18 years. The voting age is 18 years since 1989, after the 61st Amendment. 21 years was the earlier limit, 25 years is the minimum age for candidates in Lok Sabha elections, and 16 years has never been the voting age.

questions.stem_md: Which Constitutional Amendment, passed in 1988, lowered the voting age from 21 to 18 years?

options.text_md: The 42nd Amendment
The 61st Amendment
The 44th Amendment
The 86th Amendment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The 61st Amendment. The 61st Amendment lowered the voting age, with effect from 1989. The 42nd added the Fundamental Duties, the 44th removed the right to property from the list of Fundamental Rights, and the 86th added the duty on education of children.

questions.stem_md: The voters' list of the imagined village of Chandanpur names five citizens, all registered and none disqualified by law: Asha (19, graduate), Bilal (17, student), Charan (45, landless labourer), Devika (70, cannot read), and Esha (18, home-maker). Who is entitled to vote?

options.text_md: Asha, Charan, Devika and Esha
Asha and Esha only, because they are young
Asha only, because she has a degree
Charan and Devika only, because they are older

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Asha, Charan, Devika and Esha. Universal adult franchise depends on citizenship and age, not on education, property or sex, so everyone aged 18 or more may vote: Asha, Charan, Devika and Esha. Bilal is 17 and too young. The other options add conditions of age bracket, degree or seniority that the Constitution does not impose.

questions.stem_md: Which is the best reason why universal adult franchise strengthens democracy?

options.text_md: It makes sure that only experienced people become voters
Every adult has an equal say in choosing representatives, so the government rests on the consent of all
It reduces the number of elections that must be held
It gives more votes to citizens who pay more taxes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Every adult has an equal say in choosing representatives, so the government rests on the consent of all. Equal votes for all adults make the government answerable to the whole people. Voting is not limited to experienced people, the number of elections does not fall, and richer citizens do not get extra votes.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined kingdom of Zarvia, only men who own land above a fixed size may vote. Which feature of universal adult franchise is most clearly absent?

options.text_md: The holding of elections at regular intervals
The choice of a written constitution
The right of a citizen to move freely from town to town
Political equality of adults regardless of sex and property

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Political equality of adults regardless of sex and property. Barring women and those without land breaks the principle that every adult has an equal vote. Elections may still be regular, the constitution may still be written, and movement is a different matter altogether.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, how many categories of Fundamental Rights does the Constitution of India contain?

options.text_md: Six
Seven
Five
Ten

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Six. There are six categories today. Seven was the number originally, before the right to property was taken out of the list by the 44th Amendment (1978). Five and ten are not correct.

questions.stem_md: What does it mean to say that Fundamental Rights are justiciable?

options.text_md: They can be changed by the government by an order
They apply only to judges and lawyers
A citizen can approach a court to have them enforced when they are violated
They are only advice to the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A citizen can approach a court to have them enforced when they are violated. Justiciable means that a court can hear a complaint and enforce the right. They cannot be changed by a mere order, they are not meant only for lawyers, and advice to the government describes non-justiciable guidelines.

questions.stem_md: The owner of an imagined brick kiln near Mehsana keeps his workers on the site, makes them labour sixteen hours a day and pays them nothing because of an old debt. Which Fundamental Right is being violated?

options.text_md: Right to Freedom of Religion
Cultural and Educational Rights
Right against Exploitation
Right to Equality

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Right against Exploitation. Forced labour and unpaid compulsion fall under the Right against Exploitation. The facts have nothing to do with religion or minority education, and no unequal treatment between groups is described, so equality is not the best answer.

questions.stem_md: An official of the imagined district of Tarapur orders a school to close only because its managers belong to a linguistic minority that wishes to preserve its own script. Which category of Fundamental Rights would the managers cite?

options.text_md: Cultural and Educational Rights
Right against Exploitation
Right to Constitutional Remedies
Right to Freedom of Religion

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Cultural and Educational Rights. Minorities may conserve their language and script and manage their own institutions, so the managers rely on Cultural and Educational Rights. Remedies would be the route for going to court, but the right violated is the cultural and educational one; exploitation and religion are not involved.

questions.stem_md: The owner of an imagined restaurant in Kaveripur refuses to seat a customer because of the customer's caste. Which right is the owner denying?

options.text_md: Right against Exploitation
Cultural and Educational Rights
Right to Constitutional Remedies
Right to Equality

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Right to Equality. Refusing access to a public place on grounds of caste goes against the Right to Equality, which prohibits discrimination. No labour, minority institution or court action is involved in the facts given.

questions.stem_md: Which Fundamental Right allows a person to move the Supreme Court or a High Court when another Fundamental Right is violated?

options.text_md: Right to Equality
Right to Constitutional Remedies
Right to Freedom
Right against Exploitation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Right to Constitutional Remedies. The Right to Constitutional Remedies lets citizens go to the courts to enforce their other rights. The remaining three are rights that may be violated, not the right that gives the way to enforce them.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, which of the following is NOT one of the Fundamental Rights?

options.text_md: Right to property
Right to Freedom of Religion
Right against Exploitation
Right to Equality

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Right to property. The 44th Amendment (1978) removed the right to property from the Fundamental Rights; it is now a legal right under a separate provision. The three other rights are still Fundamental Rights.

questions.stem_md: During a debate in the imagined Riverside School, Anita says that Fundamental Rights are absolute, so she may say anything she likes anywhere. Which reply is accurate?

options.text_md: She is right, because no law can ever limit a Fundamental Right
Rights are subject to reasonable restrictions, for example in the interest of public order, so freedom is not unlimited
She is wrong, because rights apply only on Republic Day
She is right, because courts cannot hear cases about rights

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Rights are subject to reasonable restrictions, for example in the interest of public order, so freedom is not unlimited. The Constitution allows reasonable restrictions on several rights, such as public order and the security of the State, so the claim of an absolute freedom is wrong. Rights apply on every day, and courts can hear cases on them.

questions.stem_md: By which Constitutional Amendment were the Fundamental Duties added to the Constitution?

options.text_md: The 61st Amendment (1988)
The 44th Amendment (1978)
The 42nd Amendment (1976)
The 86th Amendment (2002)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The 42nd Amendment (1976). The 42nd Amendment of 1976 added the Fundamental Duties. The 61st lowered the voting age, the 44th removed the right to property from the Fundamental Rights, and the 86th added the eleventh duty.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, how many Fundamental Duties are listed in the Constitution?

options.text_md: Ten
Six
Twelve
Eleven

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Eleven. There are eleven, because the 86th Amendment of 2002 added one to the original ten. Ten was the number in 1976, six is the number of Fundamental Rights, and twelve is not correct.

questions.stem_md: The eleventh Fundamental Duty, added by the 86th Amendment in 2002, concerns which matter?

options.text_md: Citizens paying taxes on time
Citizens voting in every election
Citizens serving for two years in the armed forces
Parents and guardians providing opportunities for the education of children between six and fourteen years of age

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Parents and guardians providing opportunities for the education of children between six and fourteen years of age. The eleventh duty asks parents and guardians to give opportunities for education to children aged six to fourteen. Paying taxes, compulsory voting and compulsory military service are not Fundamental Duties.

questions.stem_md: A group of students scribble with chalk and tear pages out of books in the new public library of the imagined town of Haripur. Which Fundamental Duty are they neglecting?

options.text_md: The duty to respect the national anthem
The duty to develop a scientific temper
The duty to safeguard public property and give up violence
The duty to value the heritage of a composite culture

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The duty to safeguard public property and give up violence. Damaging a public library breaks the duty to protect public property. The other duties are real but are not the ones directly broken by the described behaviour.

questions.stem_md: How do the Fundamental Duties differ from the Fundamental Rights in the way they work?

options.text_md: They can be enforced by the Supreme Court in the same way as the Right to Equality
They are civic obligations that a citizen cannot directly enforce in court in the way a right is enforced
They apply only to government officers
They apply only to citizens living abroad

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** They are civic obligations that a citizen cannot directly enforce in court in the way a right is enforced. The Constitution does not provide a direct court remedy to enforce the duties as it does for rights (though Parliament may make laws on some of the matters). They apply to every citizen, in India and abroad.

questions.stem_md: Four pupils of the imagined Greenfield School list what they believe are Fundamental Duties. Which pupil has named something that is NOT in the list of Fundamental Duties?

options.text_md: To vote in every election that is held
To protect and improve the natural environment
To develop scientific temper and spirit of inquiry
To safeguard public property

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** To vote in every election that is held. Voting is a civic responsibility and a right, but it is not listed among the Fundamental Duties. Protecting the environment, scientific temper and safeguarding public property are all listed duties.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Constitution of India was brought into force on 26 January 1950 and not on the day it was adopted.

**Reason (R):** The framers wanted the date to recall 26 January 1930, when Independence Day had been observed after the declaration of Purna Swaraj.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and the reason explains the choice: enforcement was timed to recall the 1930 Independence Day, which is why it came about two months after adoption.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A citizen of India who lives in Punjab holds a separate citizenship of Punjab in addition to citizenship of India.

**Reason (R):** In the United States a person is a citizen of the nation and also of the State in which he or she lives.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false because India has single citizenship and no separate State citizenship exists. R is true, since the United States has dual citizenship.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Universal adult franchise brings political equality among adult citizens.

**Reason (R):** Every adult citizen has one vote of equal value, whatever his or her wealth, education or sex.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: because each adult counts for one vote of equal value, political equality results.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The right to property was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment in 1978.

**Reason (R):** The Constitution today lists six categories of Fundamental Rights.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both statements are true, but the second only states the count that results after the change; it does not explain why the right to property was removed, so R is not the explanation of A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution in 1976 by the 42nd Amendment.

**Reason (R):** The Fundamental Duties can be enforced by a citizen in court in exactly the same way as the Right to Equality.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true. R is false: the Constitution gives a direct remedy only for Fundamental Rights, and the duties are not enforceable in that way.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Fundamental Duties complement Fundamental Rights.

**Reason (R):** Rights can be enjoyed fully only in a society in which citizens also respect the rights of others and the common good.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: since every right depends on others respecting it, the duties of citizens are the other side of rights.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the history lesson of the imagined Lakeview School, the teacher says that the Constitution of India was adopted and came into force on the same day, 26 January 1950.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** It was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950, about two months later, so the statement is wrong.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Sunil, born in Odisha, takes a job in Kerala and must take up Kerala citizenship in addition to his Indian citizenship.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** India has single citizenship: Sunil stays a citizen of India wherever he lives, and no separate State citizenship exists.

questions.stem_md: True or false? An 80-year-old citizen of the imagined village of Pipalgaon who cannot read or write is still entitled to vote, provided she is registered.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Universal adult franchise does not require literacy, property or any other test; an adult citizen on the roll can vote.

questions.stem_md: Whichever State she lives in, a citizen of India has only ___ citizenship, and there is no separate citizenship of a State.
questions.solution_md: India has single citizenship for the whole country.

questions.stem_md: The ___ Amendment of 1988 lowered the voting age from 21 to 18, with effect from 1989.
questions.solution_md: The 61st Amendment made 18 the minimum voting age.

questions.stem_md: Fundamental Duties were added in 1976 on the recommendation of the ___ Singh Committee.
questions.solution_md: It was the Swaran Singh Committee that recommended the duties.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined situation with the category of Fundamental Rights that applies.

options.text_md: Children of one hamlet are not allowed to draw water from the common well of Barauli because of their caste
Villagers of Nandgaon are stopped, without any lawful ground, from peacefully printing a pamphlet that criticises a road project

questions.stem_md: Define a constitution and state one reason why a country needs one.
questions.solution_md: Definition and one reason.

questions.stem_md: State the dates on which the Constitution of India was adopted and came into force.
questions.solution_md: The two dates, each with its event.

questions.stem_md: Explain why 26 January was chosen as the day on which the Constitution came into force.
questions.solution_md: Link to Purna Swaraj and the 1930 observance.

questions.stem_md: Rahul, born in the imagined town of Bhavnagar, shifts to Chennai for work. Using his case, explain what is meant by single citizenship.
questions.solution_md: Meaning plus a suitable example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Single citizenship** means that all Indians are citizens of **India alone**, with no separate State citizenship. Rahul stays only a **citizen of India** after moving, and does not gain or lose a State citizenship.

questions.stem_md: How does single citizenship in India differ from the arrangement in the United States of America?
questions.solution_md: One line for each country.

answer.model_answer_md: In **India** a person is a citizen of **India only**. In the **United States** a person is a citizen of the **nation** and also of the **State** in which he or she lives, which is **dual citizenship**.

marking_scheme.step: India: citizenship of the nation only

questions.stem_md: What is universal adult franchise? State the minimum age for voting in India.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and the age.

answer.model_answer_md: **Universal adult franchise** gives every **adult citizen** the right to vote, without discrimination of caste, religion, sex, education or wealth. The minimum voting age is **18 years**.

questions.stem_md: By which amendment, and in which year, was the voting age lowered, and from which age to which?

questions.stem_md: Why are the Fundamental Rights called fundamental? Mention their justiciable nature.
questions.solution_md: Fundamental character and justiciable nature.

answer.model_answer_md: They are called **fundamental** because they are **essential for the all-round development** of the individual and are guaranteed by the Constitution. They are **justiciable**, so a citizen can **approach a court** if they are violated.

questions.stem_md: Name the six categories of Fundamental Rights as of 2024.
questions.solution_md: All six names; two marks if all six, one mark for four or five.

answer.model_answer_md: The six are the Right to **Equality**, the Right to **Freedom**, the Right against **Exploitation**, the Right to **Freedom of Religion**, **Cultural and Educational Rights**, and the Right to **Constitutional Remedies**.

questions.stem_md: A weaver of the imagined town of Kotpur is kept from working at his loom without any lawful reason. Explain how the Right to Constitutional Remedies can help him.
questions.solution_md: Access to courts and why it matters.

answer.model_answer_md: He can **move the Supreme Court or a High Court** because his Fundamental Right has been violated. The court can order that the right be respected, so the right is **enforceable** and not a mere promise.

marking_scheme.step: Citizen can go to the Supreme Court or a High Court

questions.stem_md: Which right was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights, by which amendment and in which year?
questions.solution_md: Right, amendment and year.

answer.model_answer_md: The **right to property** was removed by the **44th Amendment** in **1978**. It is now a legal right and no longer a Fundamental Right.

questions.stem_md: When and on whose recommendation were the Fundamental Duties added to the Constitution?
questions.solution_md: Year, amendment and committee.

answer.model_answer_md: They were added in **1976** by the **42nd Amendment**, on the recommendation of the **Swaran Singh Committee**. A duty on the education of children was added later, in 2002.

questions.stem_md: The residents of the imagined Lakeside Colony ask every family to keep the shared park clean so that all may enjoy it. Explain how this reflects the way Fundamental Duties complement Fundamental Rights.
questions.solution_md: Link between rights and duties.

answer.model_answer_md: Each family's **enjoyment** of the park depends on others **respecting** it, so each has a **duty** to the community. This shows that **rights come with responsibilities**.

questions.stem_md: Give three reasons why a country such as the imagined island state of Tarangia needs a constitution.
questions.solution_md: Three reasons: limits, rights, institutions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It **limits the powers** of rulers so that they cannot act as they please.
2. It **protects the rights** of citizens against misuse of power.
3. It **sets up institutions** and rules for making laws and settling disputes, giving the country **stability**.

marking_scheme.step: Sets up institutions and gives stability

questions.stem_md: Explain how single citizenship helps to promote national unity in a large federation such as India.
questions.solution_md: Same status, common identity, mobility.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. All citizens carry the **same status** wherever they live, so no one is treated as an outsider in another State.
2. It builds a **common national identity** above regional identities.
3. It makes **movement and settlement** across States easier, so people of different regions mix and unity grows.

questions.stem_md: Give three reasons why universal adult franchise strengthens democracy in an imagined constituency such as Madhupur.
questions.solution_md: Equality, answerability, participation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It gives **political equality**: every adult has one vote of equal value.
2. It makes the government **answerable to all**, so no group can be ignored.
3. It gives people a **sense of participation** and helps the government earn **legitimacy**.

questions.stem_md: Explain what makes a right fundamental and why such rights are justiciable.
questions.solution_md: Guarantee, importance, enforceability.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Fundamental Rights are **guaranteed by the Constitution**, the highest law, so ordinary laws cannot take them away.
2. They are **essential for the dignity and development** of every person.
3. They are **justiciable**: a person whose right is violated can **go to court** and have it enforced.

questions.stem_md: Name the six categories of Fundamental Rights and give one example for each.
questions.solution_md: Six categories, each with an example: half a mark for each pair.

answer.model_answer_md: **Equality** (no discrimination by caste); **Freedom** (speech and expression); **against Exploitation** (no forced labour); **Freedom of Religion** (practising one's faith); **Cultural and Educational Rights** (minorities running schools); **Constitutional Remedies** (going to court to enforce rights).

marking_scheme.step: Cultural and Educational, and Remedies with examples

questions.stem_md: List any five Fundamental Duties of an Indian citizen. (Any five, in your own words.)
questions.solution_md: Any five duties; award 1 mark for the first two, 1 mark for the next two and 1 mark for the fifth with a clear statement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. To **respect the Constitution**, the national flag and the national anthem.
2. To **protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity** of India.
3. To **promote harmony** and brotherhood among all the people.
4. To **protect and improve the environment**.
5. To **safeguard public property** and give up violence.

questions.stem_md: A pupil of the imagined Maple School says, "I have rights, so I owe nothing in return." Explain, with two reasons, why this view is mistaken.
questions.solution_md: Two reasons and a conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Rights are **enjoyed by everyone**, so each person's rights are safe only if others **respect** them; this is a duty.
2. The Constitution lists **Fundamental Duties** beside the rights to remind citizens to protect the **nation, public property and the environment**.
Hence rights and duties are **two sides** of citizenship.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A **constitution** is the **fundamental law** of a country, laying down how government is organised and what powers it has. A country needs one to **limit the power of rulers** and to **protect the rights** of citizens.

(ii) **Dr Rajendra Prasad** was the **President** of the Constituent Assembly and **Dr B. R. Ambedkar** chaired the **Drafting Committee**. The Assembly first met on **9 December 1946**.

(iii) The Constitution was **adopted on 26 November 1949** and **came into force on 26 January 1950**. The date was chosen because **26 January 1930** had been observed as **Independence Day** after the call for **Purna Swaraj**, and the framers wished to honour that pledge.

questions.stem_md:

(i) What is meant by single citizenship? **[3]**
(ii) How does the citizenship system of the United States differ from that of India? **[3]**

questions.solution_md: Meaning; contrast with the United States; unity and the OCI note.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Single citizenship** means a person is a citizen of **India alone**, whichever State he or she lives in. **No separate State citizenship** exists.

(ii) In the **United States** each person is a citizen of the **nation** and of the **State** of residence, which is **dual citizenship**. In **India** there is only citizenship of the nation, so rights do not depend on the State.

(iii) A **common status** for all gives people a **shared national identity** and makes settling in any State easy, which **binds the country together**. **Overseas Citizenship of India** is **not** dual citizenship: it gives long-term privileges but **not the right to vote**.

questions.stem_md:

questions.solution_md: Meaning and age; amendment; reasons and rebuttal.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Universal adult franchise** is the right of **every adult citizen** to vote, whatever the person's caste, religion, sex, education or wealth. The minimum age is **18 years**.

(ii) The **61st Amendment** (**1988**, effective 1989) lowered the voting age from **21 to 18 years**.

(iii) It gives **political equality**, since each adult has one equal vote, and it makes the government **answerable to all** and gives it **legitimacy**. The group's argument is wrong because a **literacy or tax test** would **exclude** the poor and the unlettered from a say in decisions that affect them, which would make the vote **unequal**.

questions.stem_md:
A class of the imagined Sunrise School studies the Fundamental Rights. Answer the following.

(i) What makes a right fundamental, and what does justiciable mean? **[3]**
(ii) Name the six categories of Fundamental Rights as of 2024 and mention the right that was removed from the list. **[3]**
(iii) Which category is violated in each of these cases: (a) a factory owner forces unpaid labour; (b) a restaurant refuses a customer because of caste; (c) a minority community is stopped from running its own school? Explain each in a line. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Fundamental and justiciable; six categories and the removed right; three cases classified.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A right is **fundamental** when it is **guaranteed by the Constitution** and essential for a person's development. **Justiciable** means that a citizen can **go to court** to enforce it.

(ii) The categories are **Equality**, **Freedom**, **against Exploitation**, **Freedom of Religion**, **Cultural and Educational Rights** and **Constitutional Remedies**. The **right to property** was removed by the **44th Amendment** (1978).

(iii) (a) **Right against Exploitation**, since forced labour is banned and a person cannot be made to work against his or her will. (b) **Right to Equality**, because discrimination on grounds of caste, especially in places open to the public, is prohibited. (c) **Cultural and Educational Rights**, because minorities have the right to conserve their language and culture and may set up and run institutions for this purpose.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) A reason for each of the three cases

questions.stem_md:
A judge of the imagined High Court of Southvale tells a school audience that a right is only as strong as the way it can be enforced. Answer the following.

(i) Why are Fundamental Rights not absolute? Give two examples of grounds on which they may be restricted. **[3]**
(ii) Explain the Right to Constitutional Remedies. **[3]**
(iii) Examine the judge's remark: explain how the justiciable nature of the Fundamental Rights makes them stronger than a mere promise, and mention one limit that remains. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Restrictions with examples; the remedies right; evaluation of the remark.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The Constitution allows **reasonable restrictions** so that one person's freedom does not harm others or the nation. Examples of grounds are **public order** and the **security of the State**.

(ii) This right lets a citizen **move the Supreme Court or a High Court** when a Fundamental Right is violated. The courts can **issue orders** to enforce the right, so it is the right that **protects all the others**.

(iii) Because the rights are **justiciable**, a victim need not depend on the goodwill of the government: an **independent court** can order the violation to stop. A mere promise has **no such remedy**. **A limit** is that rights remain subject to **reasonable restrictions**, and going to court takes **time and money**.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Approach to Supreme Court or High Court
(ii) Courts enforce and protect other rights

questions.stem_md:
The imagined Class 9 of Bluebell School prepares a poster on the Fundamental Duties. Answer the following.

(i) When, by which amendment and on whose recommendation were the Fundamental Duties added? How many are there as of 2024? **[3]**
(ii) State any four Fundamental Duties in your own words. **[3]**
(iii) Name the duty added by the 86th Amendment and explain how Fundamental Duties complement Fundamental Rights. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Origin and number; four duties; the eleventh duty and the link with rights.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) They were added in **1976** by the **42nd Amendment**, on the recommendation of the **Swaran Singh Committee**. As of 2024 there are **eleven**.

(ii) To **respect the Constitution**, the flag and the anthem; to **promote harmony** among all people; to **protect and improve the environment**; and to **safeguard public property**.

(iii) The 86th Amendment (**2002**) added the duty of **parents and guardians** to give a child between **six and fourteen** years opportunities for **education**. Duties **complement** rights: one person's rights are secure only when others **respect** them, so duties remind citizens that **rights come with responsibilities** towards the nation and society.

questions.stem_md:
During a discussion in the imagined Harmony School, a pupil says that rights are more important than duties. Answer the following.

(i) Explain two ways in which Fundamental Rights protect an individual. **[3]**
(ii) State two Fundamental Duties and say how they differ from the rights in the way they are enforced. **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate the pupil's statement by giving reasons for and against it. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Ways rights protect; two duties and the enforcement difference; balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The rights **guard the individual against unequal treatment** and misuse of power, for example through the **Right to Equality**, and they can be **enforced in court** through the **Right to Constitutional Remedies**.

(ii) Two duties are to **protect the environment** and to **safeguard public property**. Rights are **justiciable**, while duties are **not directly enforceable** in court in the same way.

(iii) **For:** rights safeguard **dignity and freedom** and have a **direct legal remedy**. **Against:** rights can be enjoyed fully only when citizens also respect others, so **duties are the other side** of rights. A balanced view is that both are **equally needed** for a healthy democracy.
